source.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
source.authors: Kenza Bouzid; Shruthi Bannur; Felix Meissen; Daniel Coelho de Castro; A. Schwaighofer; J. Alvarez-Valle; Stephanie L. Hyland

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests evidence for recoverable SAE features in a radiology-specialised multimodal model and reports results that qualify the idea that SAE features are complete, canonical units: most features score poorly under its interpretation measure, and some highly scoring features have repeated descriptions.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports SAE steering results, but those are induced interventions rather than evidence that the corresponding behaviour occurs without steering. They are recorded as findings about steering, not as evidence for the natural occurrence of a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study trains a Matryoshka-SAE on layer-15 residual activations of MAIRA-2, a 7B radiology multimodal LLM, and scores automated interpretations for 99.5% of the 16,384 features. That is a new-setting result on V4: whether a dictionary recovers interpretable sparse features in a real model. Its note of repeated descriptions among top features bears weakly on V5 (uniqueness of units). It does not show that SAE features are wrong units, so T3 fits better than the reader's T5. The steering results are induced interventions and bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find a small set of highly interpretable, clinically relevant SAE features in MAIRA-2, often finer-grained than CheXpert labels. Almost half the features were uninterpretable by their pipeline. Steering effectiveness varies by feature and case and usually produces more off-target than on-target changes. They flag possible SAE disentanglement problems: splitting, absorption or composition.
record.recipe_differences: Applies a Matryoshka-SAE to a radiology-specialised multimodal model and evaluates feature interpretation and steering; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering outcomes varied by feature and report. The paper also notes that an accidental reversal of Matryoshka group sizes appears to have slightly reduced interpretability; its impact on steering was not quantified.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-feature steering of MAIRA-2 yields mostly off-target or no changes; purely on-target changes reach at most 11.3% for any feature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering with SAE decoder directions in a domain MLLM gives weak, side-effect-laden control.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering scores for positive and negative coefficients are correlated: on-target rho = 0.90, off-target rho = 0.71. The authors read this as features staying approximately linear.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steerability of SAE features is symmetric across sign.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation frequency correlates with on-target steering score (rho = 0.40, n = 50).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frequently active SAE features are more steerable.

record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Actionable Interpretability (AIW 2025) at the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning
record.problems: Feature interpretations and steering outcomes rely on LLM-based scoring. The interpretation pipeline uses text inputs for a multimodal model. Many features scored poorly, and the authors acknowledge apparent feature repetition and possible SAE disentanglement limitations. The main text reports expansion factor 4 for downstream results, while Appendix A.2 lists expansion factor 8; the appendix also notes reversed Matryoshka group sizes and says the interpretability impact was not quantified.

untested.parts: Toy models, feature geometry, sparsity transitions: all untested.
Capacity or importance allocation of features to neurons: untested.
Whether features are spread across many neurons (no neuron-level analysis), and whether results generalise beyond one layer of one model.
Completeness (reconstruction is mentioned but not reported as a result), stability across seeds, data or sizes, and canonicality across dictionary sizes.
Comparison of one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features: untested.

missing.what: No correlation between feature density and detection F1. The densest features are poorly explained: f7633 is active on 99.3% of samples with F1 = 0.40.
Adding the image description (Findings text) to the interpretation LLM did not increase the number of interpretable features. This is a pipeline-sensitivity check on the interpretability rate.
Matryoshka group sizes were accidentally reversed; the authors say this slightly reduced interpretability, without quantifying it.

record.verdict_notes: The main text states expansion factor 4 (16,384 features), while Table A.2 lists 8; this is inconsistent. Interpretations and steering evaluation both rely on GPT-4o, and interpretations used text inputs only for a multimodal model. The steering feature set was hand-picked as a best case. The link to superposition is indirect: the paper presents itself as an SAE application, not a superposition test.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric arrangements are not tested.
The paper does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemantic neurons or whether importance allocates dedicated dimensions.
The paper does not study alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity evidences superposition.
It evaluates SAE feature interpretations in one radiology MLLM, but does not measure whether features are distributed across many neurons.
It assesses automated interpretability and repeated descriptions, not the completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features across models, datasets, or training runs.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features is made.

rows.subject: MAIRA-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured automated interpretation detection F1 for SAE features.
rows.measure: Distribution of feature interpretation detection F1
rows.baseline: 0.5 is described as random performance for a balanced evaluation set.
rows.note: Interpretations were generated and scored for 99.5% (16,299) of features. Some evaluation sets were imbalanced when 100 positive examples could not be found.
rows.check: Fine for V4. For V5 the detection-F1 distribution does not measure completeness, stability or canonicality. Low F1 may reflect the text-only interpretation pipeline, as the authors note. So for V5 this row is effectively cannot_determine. Its value (288 above 0.75, 7,500 below 0.5) matches Figure 2.

rows.subject: MAIRA-2
rows.operation_detail: Checked high-scoring feature descriptions for apparent repetition.
rows.measure: Instances of apparent repetition in feature descriptions
rows.note: The authors say repeated descriptions may indicate feature composition or splitting.
rows.check: Seven repeated descriptions among 61 features with F1 above 0.85. The authors read this as possible splitting or composition, which suggests features are not unique units. The evidence is qualitative, and there is no comparison across seeds or SAE sizes.

rows.subject: MAIRA-2
rows.operation_detail: Added an SAE decoder feature vector to residual-stream hidden states at every token position during decoding.

conditions.value: full validation set of 7,906 CXR studies

rows.measure: LLM-judged on-target and off-target changes, categorized by whether changes occurred
rows.value: 27.4% of cases had both on- and off-target changes; approximately 35% had no observable changes. Purely on-target changes reached a maximum proportion of 11.3% for a feature.
rows.note: The paper says steering usually produced more off-target than on-target changes. The reported steering is deliberately induced and does not establish the natural occurrence of the behavior.
rows.check: This is induced steering, so no version applies. The 'partial' state has no referent.

rows.subject: MAIRA-2
rows.operation_detail: Correlated steering scores for positive and negative feature coefficients.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between steering scores for positive and negative coefficients
rows.note: This compares induced steering outcomes and does not directly test whether SAE features are natural, complete representation units.
rows.check: Correlation between steering scores; no version applies.

rows.subject: MAIRA-2
rows.operation_detail: Correlated feature activation frequency with steering scores for highly interpretable features.
rows.measure: Association between activation frequency and on-target or off-target steering score
rows.value: On-target: Spearman ρ = 0.40, p ≤ 0.05, n = 50; no significant correlation with off-target scores.
rows.uncertainty: p ≤ 0.05 for the reported on-target correlation; no p-value stated for the non-significant off-target result.
rows.note: The authors excluded manually added highly activating features from this analysis.
rows.check: Correlation between activation frequency and steering score; no version applies.

relationships.condition: MAIRA-2 layer 15, Matryoshka-SAE with 16,384 features, GPT-4o detection scoring
relationships.reason: A subset of features is consistently interpretable, with clinically meaningful concepts: 288 features (1.8%) have F1 above 0.75 (R1).
relationships.display_finding: A consistently interpretable subset of features carried clinically meaningful concepts: 288 features, 1.8% of the dictionary, scored F1 above 0.75.

relationships.condition: The full feature set under a text-only automated interpretation pipeline
relationships.reason: 46% of features score below the 0.5 random level and interpretable features are rare (R1). The authors attribute part of this to pipeline limits, including that text-only scoring cannot see the images.
relationships.display_finding: 46% of features scored below the 0.5 random level, and interpretable features were rare. The authors partly blame pipeline limits, including scoring that cannot see the images.

relationships.condition: High-F1 features (F1 above 0.85) in the MAIRA-2 SAE
relationships.reason: Seven apparent duplicate descriptions among 61 top features suggest splitting or composition, so features are not unique canonical units (R2). The evidence is qualitative only.
relationships.display_finding: Seven apparent duplicate descriptions among the 61 top features suggest splitting or composition, so features may not be unique units; the evidence is qualitative only.
